What they asked us

The Wongs asked us eight questions; the first decides the rest

1Will it last?

1

Can Adrian and Carmen retire when they want, and keep the way they live?

At 65 and 62, in 2037 and 2039, on HK$780K a year CASE

  • 7

    Carmen's businessReduce, restructure or sell it over time?

  • 8

    The homeKeep it, downsize, or move district?

2Does it fit each of them?

  • 2

    Chloe's degreeHow to pay for it, here or abroad?

  • 4

    ESGHow to invest by their values, credibly?

  • 3

    The family's cryptoIs it appropriate, and how to manage it?

3What could break it?

  • 5

    InsuranceEnough for death, illness, disability, hospital, business?

  • 6

    Passing wealth onMoney and responsibility between the generations

Three parts, in this order: will it last, does it fit each of them, and what could break it.

PETE: They brought us eight questions. The first decides the rest: can Adrian and Carmen retire when they want, and keep the way they live? Two more hang on it: Carmen's business and their home. [▶] Then, does the plan fit each of them: Chloe's degree, their values, Ryan's crypto. [▶] And what could break it: their insurance, and passing wealth on. We take them in that order.

PETE: So what happens if they simply live on their investments? We played out their retirement in 10,000 simulated markets, with equities at 6% a year, inflation at 2.5% and medical costs rising with age, and we plan to Carmen's 89, the case's life expectancy. [▶] Here are ten typical futures. [▶] In seven, the money runs out before she turns 89, mostly between 76 and 88. Overall it lasts in only a third. More risk can't fix that; decisions about what they own can. Fahtai.

Will it last? · How we make it last

Four decisions about what they already own lift the odds from 33% to 83%, with no extra investment risk

Their questions12345678

Chance the money lasts to Carmen's 89, in 10,000 simulated markets MEASURED

33%

Investments alonetoday (slide 5)
1A one-person budgetagreed now: the survivor lives on 70%
2Question 7The business sold in stages2035–39, counted at HK$3.0M of HK$5.0M
3Question 8The home's value released2037: reverse mortgage or downsize
4The MPF turned into annuities2037–39: fixed, for life (HKMC)

No extra investment riskThe same investment mix in every bar

The idle 61% goes to work. What still breaks the plan in the other futures: medical bills.

FAHTAI: Thanks, Pete. The fix isn't more risk: it's four decisions about what they already own. Today: 33%. [▶] One: they agree now that after the first death, the survivor plans on 70% of the couple's budget: decided in calm, not in grief. [▶] Two, which answers question seven: Carmen sells her business in stages to her co-founder and managers. We count only HK$3 million of its five. [▶] Three, question eight: in 2037 the home's value is released, by a reverse mortgage or by downsizing; they choose at 65. [▶] Four: the MPF becomes annuities. Only one more point, but it's insurance for the worst markets. 83%, without a cent more investment risk. So what still breaks the rest? Medical bills.

Question 1, answered: they retire on time and keep the way they live.

FAHTAI: Medical bills. Slide four's premiums, kept on the Flexi plan for life, peak at HK$375K a year. [▶] So at Adrian's 75 the parents review the tier: the Standard plan costs about a third as much, and the odds rise to 97%. [▶] Then, from 2039, two spending rules: no raise after a bad year, and a 10% trim only if withdrawals run well ahead, never below 70% of the budget. Here are the same ten futures: now every one reaches Carmen's 89, and in the worst year in twenty she still spends HK$382K. That answers question one. Win.

LOOKBUA: Thank you, Win. Last part: what could break it? A plan like this only works if both incomes reach retirement. [▶] With critical-illness cover of HK$1.5 million each, individual medical cover before group cover ends, and a term-life top-up, it costs about HK$100K in year one: 14% of their surplus. [▶] And in month one they sign mirror wills with a guardian for Chloe, powers of attorney and advance directives. Then we tried to break the plan.

Us · What this means for planners like us

Wealth Management Connect is growing in both directions; for the Wongs it is a tool for later, not today

Nine mainland citiesof the Greater Bay Area

Northbound · Hong Kong and Macao residents buy mainland wealth products

Southbound · mainland residents buy Hong Kong and Macao funds and deposits

Advice only when the investor asks: no cross-boundary solicitation

Hong Kong and Macaowhere the Wongs live, earn and own

2021the scheme opens

RMB 3Mper investor since 2024, up from RMB 1M

Banks and brokerslicensed securities firms joined in 2024

Low to medium-highrisk, non-complex products only

For the Wongs: a tool for laterTheir home, income and business already sit in Hong Kong. If Adrian's work moves across the boundary, it comes in at the annual review.
For planners like us: the market we want to serveWhen a client asks, a clear and suitable answer: the product, its risks, the currency.

Under the Connect, an adviser's value is a clear, suitable answer when the client asks.

PETE: What does this mean for planners like us? Since 2021, Wealth Management Connect has let residents of Hong Kong, Macao and nine mainland cities invest across the boundary, now up to three million renminbi each. [▶] Southbound, a bank may not solicit or recommend across the boundary unless the client asks, so an adviser's value is a clear, suitable answer when asked. [▶] We kept Northbound products out of the Wongs' plan: their home, income and business already sit in Hong Kong. If Adrian's work moves across the boundary, it becomes the right tool.

P

Pete

Lead adviser

This plan taught meThree risk profiles, one family plan.

The ConnectEach client's risk matched, the currency risk made clear.

Fahtai

Retirement model

In five yearsBuilding the risk models Asia's wealth managers use for families

This plan taught meA model's job is to price the trade-offs between people.

The ConnectThe FRM next, with Connect funds as my first case.

Investment and ESG

In five yearsAn investment strategist for family clients across Asia-Pacific

PETE: In five years I want to be an investment specialist in a Hong Kong bank's wealth team, matching each client's risk, with the currency risk made clear; the Wongs were that job in miniature. [▶] FAHTAI: I want to build the risk models that wealth managers across Asia use for families. This plan taught me that a model's job is to price the trade-offs between people. Next is the FRM, with Connect funds as my first case. [▶] WIN: I want to be an investment strategist for family clients across Asia-Pacific. This plan taught me to fit each portfolio to its owner, on either side of the boundary. [▶] LOOKBUA: I plan further study in systemic risk. The Connect links two markets with different rules, so a shock in one can reach families in the other. Stress-testing this plan taught me that every risk needs a named defence.
